The market turns green for few days and suddenly the timeline is euphoric again, everyone posting their gains, everyone an expert.

Let me offer a different, more useful take: how to make the most out of the next 12 months.

First, understand where we are. This is the very beginning, not the end. When the timeline gets loud you assume it's a top signal, but the real top is when your barber, your Uber driver and your mom are asking which coin to buy. We are nowhere near that.

The single biggest mistake you can make right now is letting your bear market scars make your decisions for you.

After more than a year of everything bleeding, your instincts are broken. Every green candle feels like the top. Every 2x feels like a gift you need to grab before it disappears. So you sell, you take the small win, you feel relief, and then you watch the thing you sold do another 10x without you.

That's not risk management. That's just bear ptsd, and it will cost you this entire cycle.

In a bear market you're rewarded for caution. In a bull market you're rewarded for conviction. The hardest part is flipping your brain from one mode to the other at the right time, and most people flip far too late.

A few things that actually help:

Hold your highest conviction positions through the volatility. Your winners can run longer than you might think. Don't rotate out of a 3x into some "cheaper" play and miss the 20x.

But holding doesn't mean never taking profit. Have a plan for both directions before emotion decides for you. Sell on a plan, never on fear.

Trust the teams that shipped through the entire bear. Be far more careful with the ones that only appeared last week.

And accept that you will miss things. Coins you looked at will 50x without you. Let them go. Chasing what you missed is exactly how you buy tops.

You survived the longest bear market, which was the most difficult part. But now it’s time to make the most out of it.

Having said that, enjoy it. You earned what’s ahead of us.

All of economics is built on one assumption... scarcity.

Hyperproductive AI and hyperproductive robots break that assumption because they dissolve the old material constraints and push prices across huge parts of the economy towards zero.

Which kills the scoreboard too. GDP is a sum of whatever gets bought and sold. But as abundance drags more and more prices towards zero a bigger share of what’s really happening stops showing up in the number.

Thats the heart of my Economic Singularity framework... and @DMattin explains it wonderfully in this clip. Its what all our work at The Exponentialist is focused on.

David Sacks Calls Out Dario’s Contradictions on AI & Data Centers

@DavidSacks:

“Dario actually made this argument in the context of trying to ban export of chips, and the argument was that we want to have a data center full of geniuses in the US, and that eventually what AI's going to be used for is you're going to be able to create all these agents that are basically Nobel Prize-winning level scientists.

And if we have thousands or millions of those, and China has only dozens or 100, whatever, then we're going to win everything. And that was the whole argument.

But now we're basically banning the data centers. We're not going to have those data centers full of geniuses, and he's done his best to restrict the sale of chips to our allies as well. So I guess our allies aren't going to have the data centers either.

So we are totally shooting ourselves in the foot, and probably it would be a good thing if Dario really does believe in the data centers full of geniuses idea that he was arguing for last year, he should come forward and say, ‘We're making a big mistake by over-regulating data centers, here's how we should do it.’

I haven't heard him step up in that way, and it makes you kind of question, do you only fight for the doomer side of the argument, or are there versions of the positive side that you're willing to fight for politically?”

From my « AI practitioner » point of view new chips are crucial.

Every AI company is extremely compute constrained. Imagine I have 100 million users who want to use my product, but with the compute available today, I can only serve 10 million of them.

The obvious answer is to add more compute. But compute is physical infrastructure. Chips, memory, networking, electricity, land, permits, and construction. Every part is a bottleneck.

So let’s say we can add one gigawatt of capacity every quarter. We are doing everything possible to add more, but in the short term that supply is basically fixed.

Now imagine the next generation of chips can produce 2 to 3 times more useful tokens per megawatt. Suddenly, with the exact same electricity and data center capacity, I can serve 2 to 3 times more users. That is massive.

Better models are another lever, and those better models also depend on having better chips for training. If today I need a one trillion parameter model to complete a task reliably, but the next generation can do the same task with a 300 billion parameter model, inference becomes much cheaper. I can serve more requests with the same compute and ultimately make more money from the same subscription price.

Then there is engineering. Context compaction, better context engineering, caching etc, and moving work away from GPUs whenever possible. We spend a lot of time squeezing efficiency out of every part of the stack obviously. 

But new chips remain one of the biggest levers. When electricity is the fixed constraint, the most valuable chip is the one that turns every megawatt into the largest number of useful tokens.

That’s why I’m so excited that Vera Rubin will now be available on Azure!

tweets.text:
Reflecting on my agent stack, so much has been commoditized since May. ChatGPT and Claude can now send emails, create calendar invites, and search Google Drive. No need for a complex CLI setup or a laptop running 24/7. It all works from mobile!

The main missing piece is SMS, WhatsApp, and Telegram. That’s basically the last reason I still need Codex or Claude Code running on a laptop. I also use Computer use like right now my agent is selling a couch on Facebook Marketplace.

My wife recently subscribed to ChatGPT and connected her email, Drive, and calendar. It’s been a game changer. Our life is pretty well organized in Drive, so if she needs something about the car, finances, paperwork, etc., she can just ask and ChatGPT finds it.

Also interesting how far ahead work agents are. Copilot Cowork can use Microsoft Graph to work across Outlook, SharePoint, OneDrive, DynamicsCRM etc. and handle workflows end to end. I guess it makes sense because Enterprise customers pay more, so they get these agentic experiences first. Then they slowly make their way to consumers.
